'''Isaac David Abella''' (June 20, 1934 – October 23, 2016) was a Canadian-American physicist, cousin of [[Irving Abella]], and a professor at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name=UoC>[http://physics.uchicago.edu/research/areas/atomic_x.html "Isaac Abella"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090220191521/http://physics.uchicago.edu/research/areas/atomic_x.html |date=2009-02-20 }}, Department of Physics, University of Chicago, 2008</ref> He specialized in [[laser]] physics, quantum optics, and [[spectroscopy]].<ref name=who>[http://www.marquiswhoswho.com/libraries_researchers/default.asp "Marquis Who's Who in Science and Engineering"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080514210217/http://www.marquiswhoswho.com/libraries_researchers/default.asp |date=2008-05-14 }}, [[Marquis Who's Who]], 10th Edition 2008</ref>

==Early life and education==
Isaac Abella was born on June 20, 1934, in [[Toronto]], Ontario, Canada. He received his Bachelor of Arts degree in physics and astronomy (1957) from the [[University of Toronto]], Master of Arts (1959) degree, and Ph.D. (1963) in Physics from [[Columbia University]] in New York and studied under [[Charles H. Townes]]. Abella was involved in early research of laser development. Notably, his thesis under Townes was among the earliest works on [[two-photon absorption]].

==Career==
Abella was known for his work with laser coherent transients, employing photon echo techniques to probe metastable excited states in rare gas mixtures such as helium, neon, and argon. These states were produced in a weakly ionized RF plasma discharge. Nitrogen-pumped dye lasers were then used to generate the coherent superposition states. 

In 1969, he received the [[Quantrell Award]] for Excellence in Undergraduate Teaching from the [[University of Chicago]].<ref name="Prize">{{cite web|title=Llewellyn John and Harriet Manchester Quantrell Awards for Excellence in Undergraduate Teaching|url=https://www.uchicago.edu/who-we-are/global-impact/accolades/llewellyn-john-and-harriet-manchester-quantrell-awards-for-excellence-in-undergraduate-teaching|website=UChicago}}</ref>

Abella was also known for his work in spectroscopy of rare-earth laser materials. Specifically, samples of YLF and [[Yttrium aluminium garnet|YAG]] crystals doped with [[erbium]], [[thulium]], and [[holmium]] studied using selective laser excitation in the region of 780&nbsp;nm, the erbium bands. He studied the energy transfer process: Er to Tm, to Ho, which concentrates energy emission at 2.085&nbsp;[[μm]] at room temperature and in liquid nitrogen, a process that is a radiationless, near-resonant transfer of energy between sites that depends on the relative concentrations of the rare-earth ions. Accordingly, his experimental interests included measuring decay rates, excited state absorption, branching ratios and detailed theories of these processes.<ref name=UoC/>

==Personal life and death==
Isaac Abella died on October 23, 2016, in Chicago, Illinois, at the age of 82.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.uchicago.edu/article/2016/11/03/isaac-abella-physicist-teacher-and-resident-master-1934-2016|website=UChicago News|access-date=April 6, 2018|date=November 3, 2016|last=Borzo|first=Greg|title=Isaac Abella, physicist, teacher and resident master, 1934-2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406001409/http://news.uchicago.edu/article/2016/11/03/isaac-abella-physicist-teacher-and-resident-master-1934-2016|archive-date=April 6, 2018|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/obituaries/ct-isaac-abella-obit-20161114-story.html|website=Chicago Tribune|access-date=April 6, 2018|date=November 14, 2016|last=Megan|first=Graydon|title=Isaac Abella, University of Chicago physicist who worked with lasers, dies at 82|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406231214/http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/obituaries/ct-isaac-abella-obit-20161114-story.html|archive-date=April 6, 2018|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref>
He was married to Mary Ann Abella, Professor of Art, Chicago State University.<ref>[http://chronicle.uchicago.edu/040527/obit-abella.shtml "Mary Ann Abella"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100611013033/http://chronicle.uchicago.edu/040527/obit-abella.shtml |date=2010-06-11 }}, ''Chicago Chronicle'', Vol.23 No.17, 27 May 2004</ref> He had two children: a son, [[Benjamin Abella|Benjamin]], and daughter, Sarah.
